newsitem.title: CONGO: Congolese militia sets conditions for peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Congolese militia sets conditions for peace talks.

text.p: Heavy fighting shook Congo's capital Brazzaville for a fourth day on Sunday but a political militia fighting troops loyal to President Pascal Lissouba set pre-conditions for talks on a ceasefire.
Western military sources said armed followers of ex-president Denis Sassou Nguesso had occupied most of the city centre and surrounded the prime minister's office and treasury.
France said it would send 500 troops to reinforce the 450 already there following threats to its nationals and the death of a French soldier on Saturday.

The Congo presidency set up a mediation committee, but Ambrose Noumazalay, a spokesman for Sassou Nguesso, said his followers insisted Lissouba should admit to being the aggressor before they would agree to talks.
Troops enforcing a crackdown on private militias surrounded Sassou Nguesso's house on Thursday at the start of the fighting.

"Negotiations, even with representatives, have not yet started but we are ready. The aggressor has to recognise that he has committed a serious error before we can go to the negotiating table," Noumazalay told Reuters by telephone.
Noumazalay said Sassou Nguesso had no intention of overthrowing Lissouba but was trying to ensure political rights.
He said militia fighters were around the prime minister's office and had secured the northern suburbs of the city.
"It is not a coup d'etat, it is not a matter of saying we are here or we are there; we simply tried to repulse the aggressors, we haven't attacked, we have only responded," he said.
Parliamentary speaker Andre Milongo called a meeting of the national assembly for Monday to discuss the crisis.
Dozens of dugout canoes carrying refugees, mostly small traders originally from Kinshasa, fled Brazzaville by the "smugglers' route" across the Congo River.
The border has been technically closed on the Kinshasa side since Laurent Kabila's forces arrived in the capital of former Zaire, provoking an exodus of Hutus in the other direction.
The refugees said the Brazzaville fighting appeared to be more widespread than in 1993, when 2,000 people were killed in the capital following disputed parliamentary elections.

Brazzaville residents reported a mixture of small arms and heavy machinegun fire. One Western military source said Sassou Nguesso's "Cobras" had captured several small armoured vehicles and light tanks from the army.
The 450 French soldiers already in Brazzaville were sent there in March to evacuate foreigners from Kinshasa if necessary during the final days of the civil war in former Zaire.

French troops have intervened during army mutinies in neighbouring Central African Republic, another former colony, to evacuate foreigners and restore order. They handed over in February to an African peacekeeping force.
One French soldier was killed and five others wounded in Brazzaville on Saturday as they tried to evacuate foreigners from a building where they had been trapped by gunfire.
A senior presidency official said a mediation committee had been set up, chaired by Bernard Kolelas, the mayor of Brazzaville and Lissouba's main political opponent.
"We've already got somewhere with the political leaders, but we are having trouble getting the message across on the ground. The thing is now for the soldiers to calm down," he said.
Kolelas offered his mediation on Saturday. His "Ninja" supporters were involved in the 1993 fighting but his Bacongo district has been quiet this time.
There was no reliable death toll for the clashes although police sources spoke of several dozen dead and many wounded.
Gabonese President Omar Bongo, the region's longest serving leader, has also offered his mediation.
